title: Coupling features predict insulin-dependent diabetes
statement: Per-person coupling features alone can discriminate insulin-dependent diabetes from healthy controls with AUROC > 0.75, demonstrating that dynamic inter-organ coupling carries clinically meaningful information beyond static biomarkers.
mechanism: If glucose-HR and glucose-activity coupling reflect the integrity of autonomic and metabolic regulatory loops, then a classifier built solely on coupling features should capture enough disease-related variance to distinguish advanced diabetes from health. The coupling signature aggregates information about autonomic neuropathy, insulin resistance, and metabolic inflexibility into a compact feature set.
predictions: A classifier using only coupling features achieves AUROC > 0.75 for healthy vs insulin-dependent classification
Adding raw physiological features (mean glucose, HbA1c, etc.) to coupling features improves AUROC beyond either alone
Coupling features contribute unique variance not fully captured by raw features

literature.title: Network physiology reveals relations between network topology and physiological function
literature.key_finding: Network topology of inter-organ coupling distinguishes physiological states.
literature.relevance: Motivates the idea that coupling features form a discriminative feature space for disease classification.

feasibility.statistical_power: N=886 (668 healthy + 218 insulin) for binary classification is adequate
key_challenges: Ensuring coupling features are not proxies for raw glucose levels
dataset_limitations: Cross-sectional binary classification does not demonstrate clinical utility for screening

test_plan.primary_method: Logistic regression or gradient-boosted classifier with nested cross-validation, comparing coupling-only vs raw-only vs combined feature sets
implementation_steps: Define coupling-only feature set (all per-person correlation and entropy features)
Define raw feature set (mean glucose, HbA1c, mean HR, total activity, etc.)
Train classifiers with nested CV for healthy vs insulin-dependent
test_plan.success_criterion: Coupling-only AUROC exceeds 0.75 and combined AUROC exceeds coupling-only
test_plan.refutation_criterion: Coupling-only AUROC below 0.65, or coupling adds no incremental value over raw features
sensitivity_checks: Compare to HbA1c-alone classifier as baseline
secondary_methods: Regression analysis: coupling features predicting HbA1c (R-squared comparison)

results.method_used: Classification (coupling-only vs combined feature sets) and regression (HbA1c prediction)

sensitivity_checks.name: Combined coupling + raw features AUROC
sensitivity_checks.details: Combined AUROC = 0.952, substantial improvement over coupling-only

sensitivity_checks.name: HbA1c prediction R-squared comparison
sensitivity_checks.details: Coupling-only R2=0.144 for HbA1c prediction; combined R2=0.674. Raw features dominate HbA1c prediction.

results.interpretation: Coupling features alone achieve AUROC=0.805 for discriminating insulin-dependent diabetes from healthy controls, exceeding the 0.75 threshold. However, raw physiological features (especially HbA1c, mean glucose) dominate when combined. Coupling features capture genuine physiological information but are not a replacement for standard biomarkers in prediction tasks.
results.surprises: Coupling alone is genuinely informative (AUROC=0.805) but raw features dominate HbA1c prediction (R2=0.144 vs 0.674 combined). Coupling features add incremental value but are not transformative for pure prediction.

issues: AUROC comparison may be inflated if coupling features implicitly encode HbA1c information
Clinical utility unclear given standard biomarkers are readily available
suggestions: Test whether coupling features predict diabetes-related outcomes BEYOND what HbA1c alone predicts
Focus on coupling for mechanistic insight rather than pure prediction

notes: Coupling alone is genuinely informative but raw features dominate HbA1c prediction (R2=0.144 vs 0.674 combined). The value of coupling features is more mechanistic than predictive.
